standard.title: Events and Methods in the First Nations Civil Rights Movement
standard.description: the significant events and methods in the movement for the civil rights of First Nations Australians and the extent to which they contributed to change
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied major social and political movements and significant events in Australian history to Year 9 level, including the preconditions for civil rights activism.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate the significant events and methods in the First Nations civil rights movement and evaluate the extent to which they contributed to legal, political and social change.

nodes.label: US civil rights influence and Freedom Rides
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate the influence of the US civil rights movement on Australia and explain how it inspired the 1965 Australian Freedom Rides.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how the US civil rights movement influenced civil rights campaigners in Australia, with specific reference to the Freedom Rides.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate the effects of the US civil rights movement of the 1960s on Australia — how the Freedom Rides in the USA inspired Australian activists, particularly Charles Perkins and Student Action for Aborigines; describe the 1965 Australian Freedom Rides (route through western NSW towns, confronting segregation in swimming pools and cinemas, media coverage); explain how the Rides became a turning point in changing perspectives, beliefs and opinions in Australia.
wider: Compare the strategies of the US and Australian Freedom Rides — examining similarities in method (bus travel, confronting segregated facilities, media use) and differences in context (legal segregation vs informal/social segregation), evaluating what each strategy was designed to achieve

Investigate the media strategy of the 1965 Freedom Rides in depth — examining how Charles Perkins and Student Action for Aborigines used television and press coverage deliberately as a tool for changing public opinion

response_modes.reason: The US-Australia connection makes the Freedom Rides an ideal case for examining how civil rights movements cross national borders — and how activists deliberately adapt strategies from one context to another. This comparative frame enriches both the Australian and US civil rights histories.

success_criteria: Explain how the US civil rights movement influenced civil rights campaigners in Australia
Describe the 1965 Australian Freedom Rides, including their route, methods, and impact
Explain why the Freedom Rides are considered a turning point in the campaign for First Nations rights

nodes.label: Chronology of significant events
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can construct a chronological account of the significant events in the First Nations civil rights movement from 1962 to the Uluru Statement from the Heart.
nodes.minimum_width: Place at least five significant events in correct chronological sequence and briefly describe the significance of each.
nodes.typical_width: Create a chronological account of: the right to vote federally (1962), Freedom Rides (1965), 1967 Referendum, Tent Embassy (1972), Mabo decision (1992), Prime Minister Keating's Redfern Speech (1992), Bringing Them Home report (1997), the first Sorry Day (1998), the Apology to the Stolen Generations (2008), the Uluru Statement from the Heart (2017); for each, identify what type of change it represented (legal, political, social) or advanced.
wider: Investigate the Uluru Statement from the Heart in depth — examining the process of its creation through the 2016–2017 First Nations dialogues, its content and the Voice/Treaty/Truth framework, and the subsequent debates over constitutional recognition
Compare the 1967 Referendum campaign with the 2023 Voice referendum, examining what changed and what remained contested across more than 50 years of constitutional politics
nodes.hinge_reason: The chronological framework built here is the scaffold for Node 3's evaluative work. Students who cannot correctly sequence events and identify their type of change (legal/political/social) cannot evaluate the extent to which each event contributed to change in Node 3.

response_modes.reason: Use a structured timeline or annotated sequence activity — students need accurate knowledge of events, their dates, and their basic significance before attempting the causal and evaluative analysis in Node 3.

success_criteria: Sequence at least five significant events in the First Nations civil rights movement in correct chronological order
For each event identified, describe its basic significance and the type of change it represented or advanced
Identify at least one event in each of these categories: legal change, political change, social change

nodes.label: Evaluating the extent of change
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate the extent to which significant events and methods in the civil rights movement contributed to legal, political and social change, including the ongoing nature of Reconciliation.
nodes.minimum_width: Evaluate the extent of change produced by at least two events, using evidence to support the claim that change occurred (or was limited).
nodes.typical_width: Explain how specific events contributed to distinct types of change: legal changes from the Pilbara Strike, Palm Island Strike, Wave Hill Walk-Off, Mabo decision, Wik decision and Tent Embassy; political changes from the right to vote federally in 1962 and the 1967 Referendum; social changes from the Freedom Rides; changes toward Reconciliation from the Redfern Speech, the Bringing Them Home report, the Royal Commission into Deaths in Custody, and the Apology to the Stolen Generations; investigate the Mabo case and terra nullius; discuss how Reconciliation is not a single event but an ongoing process of truth-telling and healing.
wider: Investigate the Mabo decision and its legal significance in depth — examining how the concept of terra nullius was overturned, what Native Title means in practice, and how the decision has been applied and contested since 1992

Examine the Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody (1987–1991) as a case study — investigating what it found, what it recommended, and whether its recommendations have been implemented, as a lens on the gap between formal recognition of injustice and substantive change

response_modes.reason: Evaluating the 'extent' of change is a high-demand task. Structure it around explicit evaluative criteria — what counts as change, for how many people, how durably — and model the difference between 'this event occurred' and 'this event produced the following change, evidenced by...'.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The evaluative question — to what extent did each event contribute to change? — is directly relevant to S07 (contested historical interpretations) and offers rich opportunities for students to practise constructing evidenced historical arguments across a well-documented period of Australian history.
success_criteria: Evaluate the extent of change produced by at least two civil rights events, providing specific evidence for each
Explain the significance of the Mabo decision for understanding terra nullius and land rights
Explain why Reconciliation is described as an ongoing process rather than a completed achievement
